newsitem.title: JAPAN: Customers queue for two hours at bust Japan bank.
newsitem.headline: Customers queue for two hours at bust Japan bank.

text.p: Customers queued for up to two hours in this western Japanese town on Thursday to withdraw their money from the country's latest collapsed bank.

In a scene that has become increasingly familiar, housewives, shopkeepers and students stood in long lines outside the headquarters of Hanwa Bank Ltd, clutching bank books and discussing with each other what went wrong this time.

But there was nothing new to find in the story of 55-year-old Hanwa Bank's collapse. It simply became the 14th financial institution, including three banks, to go bust under a pile of bad loans in the past two years
Like the other failed institutions, most of Hanwa's bad loans were made in Japan's so-called "bubble" years of inflated land and stock prices in the late 1980s.

Finance Ministry figures showed Hanwa suffocating under a heap of 190 billion yen ($1.71 billion) in problem loans, against its comparatively puny capital of 20.3 billion yen ($182 million) at the end of September.
The ministry said it had suspended most business of Hanwa, a second-tier regional bank, because it was clear the company could not recover.

"This is Japan. I am sure everything will be all right. The depositor insurance system will guarantee our deposits. But I'd rather have my money back sooner, just in case," said a housewife in her 30s.

"My housing loan savings will probably be transferred to another bank in time, but it would not do any good just to leave them there for months, so I want to withdraw them now," said a worker in his early forties.
Some people joined the queues only to leave when they heard there was a two-hour wait and they could still withdraw their money on Friday.

Armoured cars transporting extra cash needed to cope with the depositors were rushed to the bank's 53 branches as it became apparent that even though there was no panic, customers wanted their money, and wanted it now. The bank has about one million accounts.
At least one rival financial institution lost no time in taking advantage of Hanwa's misfortune.

Its employees handed out brochures to people as they stood on the sidewalk waiting to get in. The brochures advertised the safety of the rival's investments as an encouragement to Hanwa customers to switch over.
Hanwa officials said nearly all of its 859 employees, including some who came back from holiday unbidden when they learned of the crisis, were helping out with the rush to withdraw savings.

The bank's new president, Zenji Watanabe, told a news conference that Hanwa's loans to the real estate sector were abnormally high, at about 30 percent of its lending, compared with only about 10 percent at other similiar-sized banks.
